content: Individuals with cystic fibrosis (CF) exhibit an increased transport of sodium across the airway epithelium. This excessive sodium absorption leads to dehydration of the airway surface liquid, which, combined with defective chloride secretion, constitutes a fundamental defect in CF. Researchers aimed to evaluate whether the topical application of sodium channel-blocking drugs could enhance respiratory outcomes in CF patients. To investigate this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register. This register includes references from extensive electronic database searches, manual reviews of relevant journals, and conference proceedings. Additionally, principal investigators, previous authors, and pharmaceutical companies involved in ion transport research were contacted for unpublished or follow-up data. The most recent search of the register was performed on December 19, 2013. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared sodium channel blockers to either a placebo, another sodium channel blocker, or the same sodium channel blocker at a different dosage. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors. However, meta-analysis was constrained due to variations in study designs. Five RCTs involving a total of 226 participants were deemed eligible for inclusion. These trials assessed the effects of the short-acting sodium channel blocker, amiloride, administered topically, in comparison to placebo. In three studies conducted over six months, a significant difference in the relative change in forced vital capacity (FVC) was observed, favoring the placebo group. The weighted mean difference was -1.51% (95% confidence interval: -2.77 to -0.25), although there was notable heterogeneity among the studies. In a separate two-week study, pre-treatment with hypertonic saline and amiloride did not yield significant improvements in respiratory function or mucus clearance when compared to pre-treatment with placebo. Furthermore, no significant differences were observed in other clinically relevant outcomes. In conclusion, the evidence does not support the use of short-acting sodium channel blockers, such as amiloride, for improving respiratory conditions in individuals with cystic fibrosis. On the contrary, there is limited evidence suggesting a potential decline in lung function associated with their use.
